:::{#thm-hazard-nonnegative}
#### A hazard is non-negative

If $\haz(t)$ is the [hazard function](#def-hazard) of a continuous random variable $T$ at a value $t$ with $\Pr(T \ge t) > 0$,
then:

$$\haz(t) \ge 0$$

:::

::: proof

For each $\change > 0$,
the ratio in the definition of the hazard is non-negative:

$$
\ba
\frac{\Pr(t \le T < t + \change \mid T \ge t)}{\change}
&\ge 0
&& \text{(a conditional probability is non-negative, and } \change > 0 \text{)}
\ea
$$

A [limit](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/calculus-derivatives.html#def-limit) of non-negative values is non-negative,
so $\haz(t) \ge 0$.

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

A hazard has no upper bound: @exm-hazard-exceeds-one has $\haz(t) = 2$,
and an exponential with a larger rate has a larger hazard.
Together with @thm-hazard-nonnegative,
the hazards of a continuous random variable range over $[0, \infty)$,
unlike the discrete-time hazard, which lies in $[0, 1]$ (@cor-discrete-hazard-unit-interval).

:::
